job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, so I sleep on a sofa bed in my sister Lucia's flat in Brightwater, with her husband Tomas and their baby, and I help with the baby in the mornings to pay my way. I did a finance degree with lots of data modules and spent eight weeks at Kestrel Bank in loan operations. Every day I use AI to tailor my CV, practise interview questions and sort my applications in a tracker. In the afternoons I tutor two school kids in maths online for twelve pounds an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's roughly what I expected, so no drama. I'd tell friends the tools are great for drafting and bad for judgement, and that's still true. Online I'd post a how-to, because I like helping people sort their job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a flat world isn't automatically a good one. Brightwater has few finance jobs, I'm on a sofa bed, and my loan is big. What helps is that I'm used to the tools, so I'm a bit ahead, but being ahead of nothing isn't much if no one's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the net: remote roles, the city two hours away and also jobs in companies that need finance people but aren't banks, like logistics firms. I'd aim for fifteen applications a week and track them in my sheet. I'd also add a third tutoring student and put aside two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient and a bit tired. I'm not scared, but I want my own room and my own pay. My sister says I'm not a burden, and I know that, but I feel it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a logistics firm want from you that a bank wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly cost tracking, invoices, forecasting and someone who isn't scared of spreadsheets and data. A bank wants a very specific kind of grad. A mid-size firm wants a person who can join and help straight away, and I can do that. The pay's lower, but the door's wider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having your own room mean in terms of money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred and fifty a month for a room, plus a deposit. I'd need a job paying at least twenty-two thousand to make it work with the loan. That's my target number, so any offer below that is a hard think.

say: I'd say the tools are **great for drafting** and bad for judgement.
Online I'd post a **how-to** on organising a job search.
think: A flat world isn't automatically good: **few finance jobs** in Brightwater and a big loan.
Being ahead on tools is worth little if **no one is hiring**.
do: Widen the net to **remote roles**, the city and non-bank firms.
Send fifteen **applications** a week and track them in a sheet.
Add a third **tutoring** student and save two hundred a month.
feel: **Impatient** and tired, wanting her own room and her own pay.
S0.quote: A mid-size firm wants a person who can join and help straight away, and I can do that.
fieldNote: Adaptive and practical: she targets **non-bank firms** where the door is wider.
Has a clear salary number, twenty-two thousand, for moving out.
Sofa-bed life weighs on her even though her sister is kind.

steps.text: Send fifteen applications a week, including remote and logistics roles
Add a third online maths tutoring student
Put two hundred a month aside toward a deposit
Keep helping with the baby mornings to pay her way

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and the smart move is to get good with it. At work I'd say show me the task and I'll show you how to do it faster. Online I'd post what I learn, because teaching helps me learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it cuts both ways. The tasks I did at Kestrel, like checking loan files and logging documents, are exactly what's moving to software, so fewer entry roles. But the people who can run the software and spot its errors will be needed, and that's me. The catch is that every graduate is trying to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small portfolio: a loan-checking workflow using AI, a forecasting model for a made-up small business, and a short write-up for each. I'd apply to roles that say analyst, operations or risk, and message people in those teams directly. I'd also take a short certificate in data analysis to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy. There's a lot of opportunity, but there's also a lot of competition from everyone doing exactly what I do. I can feel the race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stand out from graduates who do the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being specific. Instead of saying I know AI, I'd say I cut a loan checklist from forty minutes to eight, and here's the file. I'd lean on my Kestrel work and my tutoring, because teaching shows I can explain things. And I'd focus on a niche, like small business lending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firms still don't hire juniors, whatever your portfolio looks like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd freelance, helping small firms set up simple automations and reports. It's not secure, but it's something. And if that fails, I'd go back to my sister's sofa bed and take whatever pays, which I'd hate but could do.

say: I'd say **get good** with it: show me the task and I'll do it faster.
I'd post what I learn, because **teaching** helps me learn.
think: The tasks I did at Kestrel are moving to software, so **fewer** entry roles.
People who can **run and check** the software will still be needed.
do: Build a **portfolio**: a loan-checking workflow and a forecasting model.
Apply for **analyst**, operations and risk roles and message the teams.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**: lots of opportunity, but a race with everyone doing the same.
S1.quote: Instead of saying I know AI, I'd say I cut a loan checklist from forty minutes to eight, and here's the file.
fieldNote: Uses evidence over claims: a specific file, a specific number.
Her **tutoring** shows she can explain, which she plans to use as an edge.
Has a fallback of freelancing and then the sofa bed.

steps.text: Build a loan-checking workflow with AI and publish it as a portfolio piece
Apply for analyst, operations and risk roles and message the teams
Take a short data analysis certificate
Offer small firms simple reports and automations as a freelancer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change in our lifetimes and we need help right now: money for retraining, rules on how it's used, and honest talk from leaders. Two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd also say don't panic, because panic wastes time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my degree is built on exactly what AGI does. Finance analysis is thinking work, and a machine doing it better and cheaper means a very small door for graduates. Even though I'm good with the tools, so is everyone. I'd say my chances of a finance career drop sharply and I'd be looking at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid job now and save every spare penny, because cash buys time. I'd move quickly into something close to people, like care, teaching or a trade, where robots take longer. I'd sit with Lucia and Tomas and make a plan for the household, because we'd all be affected. I'd also keep tutoring, since people still want a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. There's an adrenaline kick, like before an exam, but underneath I'm scared. I'd probably chat with my sister late at night and say things I wouldn't say in daytime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots take longer. How long do you really think you have there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By the card, about three years after the thinking work, so 2031. So a trade or care job gives a bridge, not a rescue. I'd treat it as time to retrain again and save. Nobody knows what comes after, so staying flexible is the only plan I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia and Tomas about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's put everything on the table: rent, my loan, their baby costs. Tomas works at a warehouse, and I'd worry about his job too. We'd cut spending and keep a bigger emergency fund together. It would be the first time I talk to them as an equal.

say: I'd say we need **help now**: retraining money, rules and honest leaders.
I'd also say **don't panic**, because panic wastes time.
think: My degree is built on what **AGI** does, so graduate doors get tiny.
Even skilled with the tools, **everyone** else is too.
do: Take any paid job and **save** every spare penny.
Move towards care, teaching or a **trade**, where robots take longer.
Make a **household plan** with my sister and Tomas.
feel: **Shaky**: an adrenaline kick like before an exam, with fear underneath.
S2.quote: Nobody knows what comes after, so staying flexible is the only plan I trust.
fieldNote: Her tool skills do not protect her, since **everyone** will have them.
Considers hands-on work as a bridge only, not a rescue.
Brings her sister's household into the plan, so worry covers Tomas's warehouse job too.

steps.text: Take any paid job now and save every spare penny
Look at care, teaching or trade training that robots reach later
Sit down with Lucia and Tomas to set one household budget
Keep tutoring online as long as families want a person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and the people who move now will land better. At friends' gatherings I'd say learn a trade skill and a thinking skill, and keep some savings. Online I'd share resources, because there'll be plenty of anxious people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think five years gives me a chance to get a job and two or three years of experience, and maybe hop to something safer in year three. It's a race, but one I can run. The fear is that the interesting jobs vanish before I get on the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job anywhere that pays, even if it's not ideal, and use the first two years to learn the whole business. I'd save four hundred a month, work toward my own room, and pay the loan down faster. In parallel, I'd learn something robots-proof, like project management or customer-facing work, and think about what I want in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay-ish. It's like a deadline: stressful but useful. I'd probably sleep better than in the two-year version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first job that you wouldn't do in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat it like a research project. I'd ask for every kind of task, meet people in other teams, and save what I build. I'd know I'm not there forever, so I'd collect skills like coins. A normal year, I'd just do the job and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would make you move to another city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real offer with a decent salary and a team that lets me learn. I'd go in a heartbeat, even though I'd miss the baby and Lucia. Brightwater is nice but it doesn't have the roles.

I'd tell friends to learn a **trade skill** and a thinking skill.

The fear is interesting jobs **vanish** before I get on the ladder.

steps.text: Take the first paying finance or operations job and rotate through teams
Save four hundred a month toward her own room
Learn project management as a robot-resistant skill
Move cities for a good offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and a smart society uses it. I'd say schools and governments should change what they teach and help people retrain. At work I'd say let's build things that help people rather than just cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be okay. Ten years lets me get a first job, learn, move up and maybe even start my own small advisory firm for small businesses. The change would come, but I'd be ready for it. I'd just need to keep changing myself every couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job in the first six months, then pay off my loan and save into a proper cushion. I'd take a course every year, one on tech, one on people skills. And I'd probably get my own place, with my own room and a lock on the door, and maybe start an advice side project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit hopeful. It's like seeing a long road with some bends. I'd still keep an eye on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small advisory firm for small businesses actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help local shops and workshops with their books, forecasts and the AI tools that suit them. A baker doesn't need a data scientist, but she does need someone to say here's what this program does and here's what it costs. I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd worry about even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable. If a job feels safe for five years, you stop learning. I'd have to force myself to try something uncomfortable every year, like a conference or a new field.

say: I'd say a smart society **uses the time** to change what it teaches.
At work I'd say build things that **help people**, not just cut costs.
think: I'd be **okay**: first job, learn, move up, maybe my own small advisory firm.
I'd need to keep **changing myself** every couple of years.

steps.text: Take a first job within six months and pay off the loan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my whole degree is the kind of thinking work AGI does first, and two years isn't enough to retrain or move out. What would help is clear honest information, short retraining that leads to a real job, and employers still taking graduates so we can build experience.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That being good with the tools doesn't make me safe, it just makes me a faster runner in a crowded race. I'd also say thanks to my sister, because she's the cushion in all of this.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools doesn't make me safe, it just makes me a faster runner in a crowded race.
portrait: Sara, 23, has a **good finance degree** and sleeps on a sofa bed at her sister's flat.
She uses AI **every day**, builds portfolios, and applies widely, including remote and non-bank jobs.
She is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, with a clear salary target and a plan for each timeline.
She is **anxious** in most worlds because tools skill does not protect her from a crowded graduate race.
With ten years she is **uneasy** instead, and plans an advisory side firm.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most: her degree is the thinking work AGI does first.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information**, short retraining that leads to a real job, and employers still **hiring graduates**.
